Editing anything puts the results away until the next press of Calculate — change one value at a time and the updated answer tells you what that value was worth.

sections.title: How does the Shannon entropy calculator work?
sections.html:
The Shannon entropy calculator takes the values in the form, applies the relationship described below and reports shannon entropy in the results panel.

Working from the top of the form: you choose the option that describes your case (how many probabilities?); then you type in the probability 1, the probability 2, the probability 3 and the probability 4.

Press Calculate once and the page holds the relationship, tracking which boxes you filled and working out everything else; from that point on it follows every edit you make.

sections.title: What is a worked example?
sections.html:
Take How many probabilities? set to 3, Probability 1 = 10, Probability = 10 and Probability = 10. The calculator returns Shannon entropy = -66.4386 and Result = -332.1928.

Read it as a template. Every number above can be replaced with one of yours; only the relationship between them is fixed.

  1. Enter the values listed above, matching the units each box asks for.
  2. Read off the result. Any field you leave empty is the one the calculator solves for.
  3. Sanity-check the number against the relationship: Shannon entropy = -66.4386 and Result = -332.1928 should be roughly the size you expected from How many probabilities? set to 3 and Probability 1 = 10.

If a number looks wrong, check three things in this order: that the units match what you had in mind, that no drop-down is still on its default, and that the value you entered is on the same scale as the rest — a rate typed as 5 rather than 0.05 is the classic mistake. Those three account for almost every answer that is out by a factor.

sections.title: When should you use it?
sections.html:
The Shannon entropy calculator earns its place in the middle of a task, not instead of one. It is most useful when:

  • Deciding how much confidence a sample really supports
  • Turning raw numbers into something you can quote
  • Checking a result a piece of software produced
  • Any time the same 4 figures keep coming back — the probability 1, the probability 2 and the probability 3 — and you would rather not repeat the arithmetic by hand each time.

sections.title: How do you get a reliable answer?
sections.html:
• Leave the field you want solved for empty rather than guessing at it. Filling every box tells the calculator you already know the answer.
  • Write the answer down with its unit. A bare number copied into a report later is exactly where units get lost.
  • Change one input at a time when you are exploring. Two simultaneous changes make it impossible to tell which one moved the result.
  • If a result surprises you, look at the order of magnitude before the digits: a plausible number in the wrong unit looks more convincing than an implausible one, and is easier to miss.

sections.title: What else is worth knowing?
sections.html:
• Answers that depend on a drop-down reflect the option you picked, not a range. Switching to a neighbouring option is the quickest way to see how much that factor matters.
  • Some options are backed by reference tables that ship with the page, so the values are fixed data rather than a live lookup.

faq.q: What does the Shannon entropy calculator work out?
faq.a: It returns shannon entropy, derived from the probability 1, the probability 2 and the probability 3. Every field in the form feeds the same relationship: press Calculate once and changing any of them updates the result immediately, with no page reload.

faq.q: What do I need to enter to use the Shannon entropy calculator?
faq.a: The form asks for the probability 1, the probability 2, the probability 3 and the probability 4, which is 11 fields in total. Each one is labelled with what it means and, where relevant, the unit it expects. Anything you leave blank is treated as the value to solve for.

faq.q: How much do the drop-down choices change the answer?
faq.a: There is one choice to make (1 in total), and each one selects a different case rather than scaling the result. Switching a single option and watching the result is the fastest way to see how much that choice is worth.

With the values the page starts from, the calculator reports Shannon entropy = -66.4386. Treat that as a reference point rather than a recommendation: it exists so you can tell at a glance whether your own inputs are on the same scale.

faq.q: Is the Shannon entropy calculator free to use?
faq.a: Yes — no account, no sign-up and no limit on how many times you run it. The arithmetic happens in your browser, so the values you type are not sent anywhere.

faq.q: Do I have to fill in every box?
faq.a: Fill in the ones you know. The result boxes are computed from them, so you never enter a value the formula can derive — press Calculate and every result updates together.
